cf.title: [CREATE|RE] INDEX CONCURRENTLY with single heap scan

verdict_reasoning: Demand is shown and reviewers support the STIR design, so nothing fails at level 1. The surviving objections are fixable level 2 points, and prior-attempts-1 is decisive: validation refreshes its snapshot, and the thread states no invariant that excludes the missing-tuple failure recorded in P5. maintenance-fit-1 and replication-ondisk-1 add two uncovered paths. A committer who knows HOT pruning and concurrent index builds has to accept the safety argument.

brief.title: Single heap scan for CREATE INDEX and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY using STIR auxiliary index
brief.problem: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY and REINDEX CONCURRENTLY scan the table twice and hold long-lived snapshots, so they are slow and hold back the xmin horizon. VACUUM on every table in the database then cannot remove dead tuples. An earlier fix (commit d9d076222f5b, PG14) that let VACUUM ignore such backends was reverted after a bug that left tuples missing from indexes.
brief.proposed_design: Before the build, the patch creates an unlogged auxiliary index of a new STIR access method; it stores only the TIDs of tuples inserted during the build. Validation replaces the second heap scan: it merges sorted TIDs from STIR and the target index, then fetches and inserts the missing tuples. A later patch refreshes the validation snapshot every 100ms (earlier versions used every 4096 pages); snapshot resets in the first scan moved to CF entry 6401.
user_visible_surface: New index access method `stir` in pg_am, with opclass and opfamily; `CREATE INDEX ... USING stir` fails with "Building STIR indexes is not supported".
Failed builds leave an invalid auxiliary index named with suffix `_ccaux`, shown by psql `\d`; DROP INDEX on the main index drops it.
pg_stat_progress_create_index: new phase "waiting for writers to use auxiliary index", and "index validation: scanning table" becomes "index validation: merging indexes" with tuple counts.
C API: `index_create()` gets new parameters (relpersistence, auxiliary index link), `IndexInfo.ii_Auxiliary`, `IndexVacuumInfo.validate_index`, and Datum storage in tuplestore.
Documentation states that concurrent builds have minimal impact on VACUUM of other tables.
author_claims: Index builds run about 2 to 4 times faster; one pgbench test went from 117 s to 68 s.
Concurrent pgbench throughput is not affected, and the oldest snapshot age stays near zero during the build.
The STIR index is small (typically under 1 MiB), writes no WAL, and has no measurable insert overhead.
Stress tests and a reviewer's banking-style consistency test found no missing tuples.
Index AMs need no extra work to benefit.
brief.thread_state: Matthias van de Meent, Heikki Linnakangas and others support the STIR approach, and logical decoding alternatives were rejected. Matthias reviewed 0002 and 0003 in August 2026 and promised a review of 0004 onward; v40 has had no reply, and CFbot reports it needs a rebase.
unclear: The material does not explain why the snapshot refreshes during validation are safe against HOT pruning, which caused the PG14 revert.
No benchmark shows bloat reduction on an update-heavy table, which Matthias asked for.
The material does not say how the new snapshot refreshes interact with the snapshot-reset series in CF entry 6401, beyond an open TODO for skipped TIDs.
Behaviour for third-party index AMs and for crash recovery with a leftover `_ccaux` index is not described.
STIR insert lock contention under heavy concurrent writes has no reported numbers after the v38 multi-page change.

prior_attempts.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance
prior_attempts.quote: These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index creation.
prior_attempts.reason:
This reverts commit d9d076222f5b "VACUUM: ignore indexing operations
with CONCURRENTLY".

These changes caused indexes created with the CONCURRENTLY option to
miss heap tuples that were HOT-updated and HOT-pruned during the index
creation.  Before these changes, HOT pruning would have been prevented
by the Xmin of the transaction creating the index, but because this
change was precisely to allow the Xmin to move forward ignoring that
backend, now other backends scanning the table can prune them.  This is
not a problem for VACUUM (which requires a lock that conflicts with a
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY operation), but HOT-prune can definitely
occur.  In other words, Xmin advancement was sped up, but at the cost of
corrupting the resulting index.

Regrettably, this means that the new feature in PG14 that RIC/CIC on
very large tables no longer force VACUUM to retain very old tuples goes
away.  We might try to implement it again in a later release, but for
now the risk of indexes missing tuples is too high and there's no easy
fix.

Backpatch to 14, where this change appeared.

Diagnosys-by: Michael Paquier <michael@paquier.xyz>
Diagnosys-by: Andres Freund <andres@anarazel.de>
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P5 let VACUUM and pruning ignore the CIC backend's xmin. This proposal keeps a real, periodically refreshed snapshot and uses STIR to collect new TIDs in place of the second heap scan.

prior_attempts.title: avoid bloat from CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
prior_attempts.quote: However, now that I read the patch: this is a horribly ugly hack.
prior_attempts.reason: Tom Lane objected to the new, undocumented snapmgr API and proposed instead to make index AMs responsible for popping the snapshot. Simon Riggs answered that he had chosen the snapmgr API because an index AM that pops the snapshot wrongly would cause a crash, and he offered to follow consensus. The visible messages show no further discussion before the entry was returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P3 released the snapshot only after the first scan, btree only, through a new snapmgr API. This proposal refreshes snapshots during validation and replaces the second scan with STIR.

prior_attempts.title: Skip all-visible pages during second HeapScan of CIC
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P13 made the second heap scan cheaper by skipping all-visible pages. This proposal removes that scan and merges STIR TIDs with the target index.

objections.title: Validation snapshot refresh needs a stated argument against the PG14 failure
objections.failure_scenario: During validation, CIC drops its old snapshot every 100ms, so other backends HOT-prune pages behind it. If a chain root that STIR or the target index depends on is pruned between refreshes, the new index misses a live row. Users see this later as wrong query results or an amcheck failure.
objections.argument: The PG14 revert [P5] was caused by HOT pruning that moved forward once the CIC backend no longer held back xmin; 0007 brings back a moving xmin in the validation phase. Message #74 says resets are safe because only TIDs recorded in STIR are compared, but gives no invariant or proof. Message #3 asked for a formal argument, and the stress tests in messages #69 and #43 are evidence, not proof. Message #125 also leaves an open TODO for TIDs the build skipped.
objections.author_must_show: Which invariant ensures that every live tuple missing from the target index has its HOT-root TID in STIR, even when pruning runs between validation snapshot refreshes?

precedents.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance

critic.reasoning: Message #74 asserts that validation resets are safe against HOT pruning but states no invariant, and the brief lists this as unexplained. P5 records the same failure class, so the precedent applies and a written argument is a fair request.

objections.title: Validation correctness depends on a second, separately reviewed patch series
objections.failure_scenario: CF entry 6401 (snapshot resets in the first scan) and this series are committed in different releases. The open TODO from message #125 is not carried over. Tuples skipped by the build's duplicate-check budget never reach STIR or validation, so the finished index lacks them and nobody notices until a query returns wrong results.
objections.argument: Message #125 says that once the series are combined, skipped TIDs "must also reach validation, as STIR alone may miss them", and leaves a TODO for it. The completeness invariant of the index then spans two CF entries that share snapshot helpers and an interval setting. A committer of either entry must keep the other's assumptions in mind, and no test is named that fails if they diverge. The same class of bug, tuples missing from a concurrently built index, caused the PG14 revert [P5].
objections.author_must_show: Which check or test fails if 6401 lands without the skipped-TID handoff, and in which entry does that handoff live?

precedents.title: Revert changes to CONCURRENTLY that "sped up" Xmin advance

critic.reasoning: Message #125 says that skipped TIDs must reach validation when the two series are combined, and leaves this as a TODO. The material names no test or owning entry for that handoff, and missing index tuples is the failure class recorded in P5.

objections.title: Leftover unlogged STIR index on a logged table across persistence-changing commands
objections.failure_scenario: A failed CIC leaves `idx_ccaux` as an unlogged index on a permanent table. A DBA later runs `alter table ... set unlogged` and then `set logged`, or `vacuum full`, `cluster` or `truncate`, before dropping it. These commands rebuild every index with the table's persistence, so the STIR either becomes WAL-logged against its `!RelationNeedsWAL` assertions or hits "Building STIR indexes is not supported".
objections.argument: Before this patch an index always had its table's persistence. Message #123 makes the STIR always unlogged on purpose and adds a `relpersistence` parameter to `index_create()`, so mixed persistence becomes a state that can persist on disk. Patch 0005 covers DROP and REINDEX of a junk `_ccaux`. The material does not say what the other rewrite paths do with it, and `_ccaux` survives until someone drops it.
objections.author_must_show: What do SET LOGGED, SET UNLOGGED, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and TRUNCATE do to a leftover `_ccaux` index, and which tests cover each path?

critic.reasoning: Message #123 confirms that STIR is always unlogged, even on a permanent table. Patch 0005 covers only DROP and REINDEX, and TRUNCATE, CLUSTER and VACUUM FULL rebuild indexes through the build path, which STIR rejects.

objections.title: A stub index AM in pg_am that every AM-wide change must special-case
objections.failure_scenario: A future patch adds a new index AM callback or a new code path that loops over indexes, such as ANALYZE, VACUUM, pgstattuple or amcheck. It does not handle STIR's stub behaviour. A leftover `_ccaux` index then raises an error or an assertion, as the unclosed critical section did during ANALYZE in message #62, and users find out only in the field.
objections.argument: The series registers `stir` in pg_am with an opclass and opfamily, and special-cases it in analyze.c, vacuumlazy.c, vacuumparallel.c, pgstattuple and opr_sanity. Heikki in message #106 proposed a shared memory struct instead of using the catalog for this coordination. Message #107 answered with relcache-synchronization concerns, and the thread did not settle which design leaves fewer places to update. The material does not say what makes a future change fail loudly when it forgets STIR.
objections.author_must_show: What makes a new index-wide code path fail in regression tests, not in production, when it does not account for a STIR index?

critic.reasoning: The patch special-cases STIR in analyze.c, vacuumlazy.c, vacuumparallel.c and pgstattuple, and message #62 shows one such path already failed on a leftover index. Messages #107 and #108 answer the shared memory alternative but not how a forgotten special case fails in tests.

objections.title: Docs promise minimal VACUUM impact before the series delivers it
objections.failure_scenario: A DBA reads the new CREATE INDEX and REINDEX text that concurrent builds have minimal impact on VACUUM of other tables. The DBA then runs a long CIC on a large table. The first heap scan still holds one snapshot, because the first-scan resets now live in CF entry 6401, so the xmin horizon stays behind for the whole build and other tables bloat.
objections.argument: The documentation hunk comes from the full series, but message #74 removed the first-phase snapshot reset from this entry. Message #125 says the two series work independently and still leaves a TODO for skipped TIDs. If this entry is committed alone, the user-facing contract claims more than the code delivers, and that wording is hard to take back once released.
objections.author_must_show: What exactly will the CREATE INDEX and REINDEX docs promise about VACUUM if this entry is committed without CF entry 6401?

critic.reasoning: Message #74 moved the first-scan resets out of this entry, and the only documentation hunk shown still promises minimal impact on VACUUM. This is a wording fix and not a permanent commitment; the v40 documentation text is not in the material.

refuted.title: Progress view phase and columns change meaning for existing monitors
refuted.failure_scenario: An operator's dashboard follows `pg_stat_progress_create_index` with `phase = 'index validation: scanning table'` and `blocks_done/blocks_total`. After upgrade, the phase string no longer appears and the block columns stay at zero during validation. The dashboard shows a stalled or missing phase, and the operator learns this during a production reindex.
refuted.argument: The 0008 monitoring hunk renames a documented phase and moves its progress from block counters to tuple counters. It also adds a new phase before the build. Progress views are an interface that tools parse, and the proposal does not discuss keeping the old phase name or listing the change as an incompatibility in the release notes. A committer would likely ask for that to be weighed explicitly.
refuted.author_must_show: Why should the existing validation phase be renamed and switched to tuple counters rather than keeping its name and adding a new phase, and how will release notes flag it?

critic.reasoning: The validation phase no longer scans the table, so the old phase name and block counters would report something that does not happen. The monitoring hunk documents the new phase and tuple counters; the release-note wording is outside levels 1-2.

refuted.title: Catalog-visible stir AM exposes an object users cannot recreate
refuted.failure_scenario: A CIC fails and leaves `idx_ccaux` with `stir` in `\d`. A schema-diff or migration tool copies the definition with `pg_get_indexdef()`, then runs `CREATE INDEX ... USING stir` on another server. That command fails with "Building STIR indexes is not supported", and the user finds out when the tool aborts.
refuted.argument: The patch adds a row to pg_am plus an opclass and opfamily. They appear in `\dA`, `\d` and pg_get_indexdef(), but the only answer to CREATE is an error. In message #106 Heikki suggested tracking the build in a shared memory struct to avoid an ephemeral index AM in the catalog, and the reply in message #107 did not settle the user-visible side. In messages #117 and #120 a reviewer found two INVALID indexes confusing to recover from.
refuted.author_must_show: How do pg_get_indexdef(), `\dA` and schema tools treat a leftover stir index, and why must the auxiliary structure be a catalog-visible AM at all?

critic.reasoning: pg_dump skips invalid indexes, and a tool that copies an INVALID index definition gets a clear error, which is not a data or upgrade failure. Messages #107 and #108 weighed the shared memory alternative; maintenance-fit-2 covers the remaining catalog cost.

refuted.title: STIR skip-insert state is lost on crash or standby promotion
refuted.failure_scenario: The primary crashes, or a standby is promoted, while a CIC is between validation and dropping the auxiliary index. Unlogged-relation reset restores the STIR from its init fork, so any skip-insert mark (`StirMarkAsSkipInserts`) is gone while the catalog still says the index is ready. Every later insert on the new primary appends TIDs to `idx_ccaux` until a DBA notices and drops it.
refuted.argument: Message #62 shows that part of the STIR lifecycle state lives on an unlogged page, and the commit message says the auxiliary index is marked ready through the catalog, which is WAL-logged and replicated. After a crash or failover the two sources of truth can disagree, because only the catalog survives. The brief lists crash recovery with a leftover `_ccaux` as not described, and the material has no test for promotion during a build.
refuted.author_must_show: After crash recovery or standby promotion in the middle of a build, what makes backends stop inserting into a leftover `_ccaux` index, and which test exercises this?

critic.reasoning: After a crash or promotion the build is dead, and the result is an invalid `_ccaux` index that still receives cheap TID inserts until dropped. The documentation hunk already describes this state and its recovery, as for `_ccnew` today.

refuted.title: New per-insert work for all writers of a table under CIC
refuted.failure_scenario: A DBA runs REINDEX CONCURRENTLY on a hot table with hundreds of concurrent inserting backends. Each insert now takes an exclusive buffer lock on a shared STIR page during the whole first phase. Application latency rises for the length of the build, and the DBA sees it only under production load.
refuted.argument: Today CIC adds no insert work before the new index becomes indisready. With STIR, every insert during the build goes through stirinsert, which message #122 describes as serializing all insertions on exclusive locks. v38 spreads inserts over several pages (message #124), but the author calls that version not yet convincing, and the material reports no contention numbers after it. The cost falls on every CIC user, because the new path replaces the old one with no way to opt out.
refuted.author_must_show: What is insert latency and throughput with v38 under many concurrent writers during CIC, compared with master?

critic.reasoning: Messages #43 and #46 report unchanged pgbench throughput at 8 and 50 clients while building an index on `abalance`, where every update inserts into STIR. Those runs used the single-page design, and v38 only reduces that contention; the cost falls only on tables under CIC.

touch_points.reason: A failed build leaves an unlogged `_ccaux` STIR index on disk, attached to a permanent table.

touch_points.label: WAL / replication / standby
touch_points.reason: The STIR index writes no WAL, but its catalog state is WAL-logged and replicated.

touch_points.reason: The patch adds `stir` rows to pg_am, pg_opclass, pg_opfamily and pg_proc, and a new dependency link.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: `index_create()` gets new parameters; IndexInfo, IndexVacuumInfo, tableam.h and tuplestore change.

touch_points.label: psql UX conventions
touch_points.reason: psql `\d` shows a second INVALID index, `idx_ccaux` with AM `stir`, after a failed build.

touch_points.reason: A new index AM is special-cased in ANALYZE, VACUUM, parallel vacuum and pgstattuple, and correctness is shared with CF entry 6401.

touch_points.reason: Every insert into a table under a concurrent build also inserts a TID into the STIR index.

questions: Which invariant ensures that every live tuple missing from the target index has its HOT-root TID in STIR when pruning runs between validation snapshot refreshes?
Which CF entry owns the handoff of TIDs skipped by the build to validation, and which test fails if entry 6401 lands without it?
What do SET LOGGED, SET UNLOGGED, VACUUM FULL, CLUSTER and TRUNCATE do to a leftover unlogged `_ccaux` index on a permanent table?
What makes a new index-wide code path fail in regression tests when it does not account for a STIR index?
What will the CREATE INDEX and REINDEX documentation say about VACUUM if this entry is committed without CF entry 6401?

committability.owner_note: Heikki Linnakangas supported the STIR approach in the thread, but v40 has no reply. The owner must know HOT pruning, snapshot and xmin handling, and the concurrent index build code.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the completeness of every concurrently built index, the failure class that forced the PG14 revert (P5). The owner also carries a permanent `stir` AM in the catalog and its special cases in VACUUM and ANALYZE.
committability.author_follow_up: Strong sign: the author has rebased the series through 12 CommitFests up to v40 and answers review.

priority.reason: Operators of large, busy tables gain faster concurrent builds and a moving xmin horizon, and several reviewers asked for this. The series is large, adds a catalog AM and touches heap, nbtree, catalog and vacuum code; it needs a rebase and a written safety argument.

provisional_note: Only v16 patch prose and 3 of 126 messages were read; v40 may already answer some points. Whether the TID merge and snapshot refresh are safe against HOT pruning cannot be judged without the code.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on partitioned table
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch lets create index concurrently work on partitioned tables by first creating catalog entries for all partition indexes with indisvalid=false, then building each one concurrently. An interrupted run leaves invalid indexes that the user can clean up with DROP or REINDEX, as with CIC on a plain table.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last shown message, from Alexander Pyhalov in July 2023, asks whether releasing the session lock on the parent table between child index builds is safe, and no reply is shown. No committer review appears in the thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY on partitioned index
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY support for partitioned indexes. It changes index_drop() to expand a partitioned index into the list of its partition indexes and run the concurrent drop steps on all of them in two transactions.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Michael Paquier disliked the new code path for deleting dependent objects in the partition tree and said the problem needed more design work first. The patch then stopped applying to HEAD, and the author withdrew it until the related patch for CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY on partitioned tables makes progress.

precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch releases the snapshot that create index concurrently takes for the first-phase table scan once the scan ends, so the sort and build phases do not hold back the global xmin and vacuum can control bloat in other tables. It covers btree only, through a new snapmgr API.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane objected to the new, undocumented snapmgr API and proposed instead to make index AMs responsible for popping the snapshot. The visible messages show no further discussion before the entry was returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: remove spurious CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY wait
precedents_retrieved.summary: Let CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY set a PGPROC flag so that other CICs skip it in WaitForOlderSnapshots, and so do not wait for the slowest concurrent CIC to finish. After review, the patch was narrowed to a PROC_IN_SAFE_CIC flag, set only for indexes that are neither on expressions nor partial.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Tom Lane objected that expression indexes can run user-defined functions, as ANALYZE does. The author answered by narrowing the patch to non-expression, non-partial indexes, and the last message is a favorable review from Michael Paquier.

precedents_retrieved.title: Avoiding deadlock errors in CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch removes the third wait in create index concurrently, the wait for transactions with older snapshots at the end of phase 3, so that concurrent DDL on the same table no longer fails with deadlock errors. It sets indcheckxmin when the index is marked ready and makes pg_index updates transactional so older snapshots cannot use the new index.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch was returned with feedback for lack of activity after it had waited on the author for more than two weeks. Michael Paquier doubted that the transactional pg_index update is safe and asked whether all cache lookup failures were fixed. Yoshikazu Imai pointed to comments describing the create index concurrently method that need changes, and the visible messages show no reply from the author.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
And while looking at this patch, I have doubts that what you are doing
is actually safe either.

precedents_retrieved.title: Use tuple-level SIREAD locks for index-only scans
precedents_retrieved.summary: Index-only scans that skip the heap would take tuple-level SIREAD locks instead of locking the whole heap page, with a fix to the outdated comment in nodeIndexonlyscan.c. A later experimental patch also skipped the btree page lock when the scan uses equality quals on all key columns of a unique index.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The patch stopped applying after a collision in the test files, and Daniel Gustafsson asked for a rebased version. No new version appears in the visible messages, so the entry was returned with feedback. Earlier, David Rowley found that deferrable unique constraints broke the btree lock skip, and Thomas Munro fixed that case in v4. Thomas Munro was still unsure the fix covered every case.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This patch now fails to apply, probably due to a mostly trivial collision with fdd88571454e2b00dbe446e8609c6e4294ca89ae in the test files.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add index scan progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds index vacuum progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum, with counts of indexes to process and indexes processed, including indexes handled by parallel vacuum workers. Later versions keep worker progress in a hash table in the main shared memory segment, so the progress views can read it after a worker exits.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Robert Haas objected to the use of the main shared memory segment and to the locking it adds to progress reporting, which is meant to be low overhead. They asked that workers pass data to the leader through the parallel vacuum's dynamic shared memory, and that the leader report it with the existing progress fields; Masahiko Sawada agreed. Greg Stark returned the patch because of these design changes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That is, I am imagining that you would want to use DSM to propagate
data from workers back to the leader and then have the leader report
the data using the existing progress-reporting facilities.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add support for ALTER INDEX .. ALTER [COLUMN] col_num {SET,RESET}
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add `alter index ... alter [column] col_num set/reset (...)` so opclass parameters on an index column can be changed after `create index`, using a column number as `set statistics` does. The patch stores the new values in pg_attribute attoptions, checks them with index_opclass_options(), and does not rebuild the index.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Changing an opclass parameter such as siglen without a rebuild leaves the index inconsistent with its options. Nathan Bossart reproduced test failures in hstore after `alter index hidx alter column 1 set (siglen=100)`, which went away after a REINDEX. Alexander Korotkov said the known uses for opclass options all need a rebuild and suggested keeping the options immutable until real cases for mutable ones appear. The author agreed the patch was not enough, and the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: All these cases require index rebuild to change the opclass option.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This test was trying to test the mechanism to release kernel FDs as needed
to get us under the max_safe_fds limit in case of spill files.  To do that,
it needs to set max_files_per_process to a very low value which doesn't
even permit starting of the server in the case when there are a few already
opened files.  This test also won't work on platforms where we use one FD
per semaphore.

roaster_notes.note: Only one objection: the precedents mostly targeted the same goal by other means, and their recorded reasons, apart from the PG14 pruning revert, do not apply to the STIR design.

The SQL syntax does not change and there are no new keywords, and pg_dump does not appear to emit invalid indexes, so the round trip is not affected. The objections above are fixable and do not reject the idea.

WAL volume, hot standby queries, base backups and pg_dump look unaffected: STIR writes no WAL, and invalid indexes are neither used by queries nor dumped. The init-fork WAL logging issue from message #122 was fixed in message #123.

The proposal changes no privilege rules. Concurrent builds still need the same ownership and locks, and `CREATE INDEX ... USING stir` is refused. Index expressions still run as the table owner, under the same restrictions as before. STIR grows only with the tuples inserted during the build, so its size follows the heap's growth, which needs no extra privilege. Not checked without the code: whether the `_ccaux` index inherits the main index's owner, tablespace and dependency entries.
Not empty. The nbtree VACUUM-bookkeeping invariant does not apply: validation only collects TIDs and deletes no pages.

Postgres has no existing feature that gives a concurrent index build with one heap scan and no long-held snapshot. Plain CREATE INDEX blocks writes, and the PG14 horizon shortcut was reverted [P5]. The logical-decoding alternative was discussed and rejected in messages #89, #100, #101 and #106, and no extension or hook in the material does the job. Whether STIR should be a pg_am entry or an internal structure (message #106) is a design question for another angle.

The material shows real, lasting demand: the PG14 feature for the same goal was called "extremely valuable for users" when it was reverted [P5], and several independent people (Matthias, Heikki, Sergey, Josh, Antonin) say they want it or test it on busy systems (messages #45, #56, #69, #106, #117). The costs (a new catalog AM, an index_create() API change, two invalid indexes after a failure) are design and maintenance questions for other angles.
